newsitem.title: USA: New T. Rowe Price fund offers simple way to invest.
newsitem.headline: New T. Rowe Price fund offers simple way to invest.

text.p: In January, T. Rowe Price introduced a new mutual fund that will provide investors with easy access to an array of overseas markets.

Together with another pair of the company's funds, this new entry makes it simple for investors with modest savings and little knowledge of the financial markets to compile more diversified fund portfolios.

The new fund is the T. Rowe Price Spectrum International Fund (800-638-5660; $2,500 minimum investment; no-load). It seeks long-term capital appreciation by investing in as many as nine T. Rowe Price stock and bond funds and a money market fund.

The fund's management committee will adjust the mix of funds over time to adapt to conditions in financial markets around the world. For example, when Japanese stocks look promising, they might nudge up the fund's stake in the Japan Fund -- but not by much.

"The managers will make only modest shifts among the funds over a period of many months," said Steve Norwitz, vice-president of T. Rowe Price Associates. "It's not their policy to make big, dramatic bets on any one country's market."

Why launch a new international fund when overseas stocks have been trailing the U.S. market? In fact, the timing could turn out to be excellent. Many analysts believe that overseas stocks are due to catch up with U.S. equities in the next year or two as our stock market takes a well-deserved breather.

The fund, managed by Rowe Price-Fleming International, will serve as a counterpart to a pair of other Price funds. The first, T. Rowe Price Spectrum Growth, has delivered 30 percent higher returns than the typical equity fund during the past five years, but has only been about 70 percent as volatile, according to Morningstar Inc.

Spectrum Growth invests in a mix of six equity funds and one money market fund. The stock funds cover a broad range of equity sectors, including small-company stocks, growth stocks, value-oriented stocks, shares that pay high dividends and international stocks. Recently, the highest stake was a 23 percent investment in T. Rowe Price Growth Stock Fund. The lowest: 11.7 percent in T. Rowe Price New Era.

The T. Rowe Price Spectrum Income Fund takes a similar approach to investing in fixed-income markets. It divides its money among funds that invest primarily in fixed-income assets. Recently, it held a 30 percent stake in the New Income fund -- which invests in a mix of government and corporate bonds.
It also invested around 7 percent of assets in T. Rowe Price International Bond Fund. Spectrum Income also invests a modest amount in a fund that holds high-yield stocks, T. Rowe Price Equity-Income.

Result: the fund has gained 9.1 percent annually during the past five years, compared with 7.2 percent for the typical intermediate-term bond fund. Moreover, Spectrum Income has been less volatile than its average competitor.

The Spectrum funds are examples of a breed called "funds of funds" -- mutual funds that invest in a portfolio of other funds. Such funds of funds make sense for beginning investors who don't have the money to invest the typical $1,000 to $3,000 minimum investment in four or five funds.

In addition, funds like the Spectrum entries provide a hand-picked portfolio of funds for investors who don't feel comfortable making those choices on their own. Moreover, the funds' managers can keep tabs on market conditions and make appropriate changes from time to time.

Of course, those changes might actually cause shareholders to lose money or miss opportunities. Worse, some funds charge heavy expenses. Such costs can include a management fee charged by the fund company that compiles the portfolio, as well as fees for the individual funds in the portfolio.

But the Spectrum entries avoid both problems. First, they make only modest adjustments in their fund mixes, so that an occasional mistake doesn't weigh too heavily on long-term results. They also tend to shift money into funds that have been trailing the market and offer better value than high flyers. That value-oriented approach tends to reduce risk.

Second, the funds invest only in other T. Rowe Price funds, which don't charge it for expenses. Thus, total annual expenses range from about 0.8 percent to around 0.9 percent for both Spectrum Growth and Spectrum Income. The new Spectrum International Fund's expenses are expected to range between 0.83 percent and 1.37 percent of assets.

Some investors might prefer not to be limited to one family's funds. In that case, you can use the Spectrum funds as a base for your portfolio -- then add your favourite choices from other sponsors. Just be sure that the final mix makes sense in terms of your goals and risk tolerance.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers mutual funds for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
